tiers: Permitted on certain assignments with acknowledgment
documents.summary: TLC syllabus guidance asks instructors to state a generative AI policy and offers three model statements from permitted to prohibited. All require acknowledgment or flag academic dishonesty, and each notes that other courses may differ.
documents.stance_why: The page asks 'What is your policy on how students should engage with generative AI' and supplies three model statements (permitted, permitted on certain assignments, 'strictly prohibited'), so the stance is left to each instructor with templates, i.e. delegates.

units.policy: Instructors provide the rationale behind course policies and frame expectations in positive, action-oriented language.

documents.title: GP-004.02 Acceptable Use of Generative AI
documents.summary: An IT-security standard on responsible use of generative AI. It focuses on data classification, with restrictions on confidential data, and adds advice on verification, disclosure expectations and bias. It says little about academic coursework.
documents.stance_why: The standard gives guidance for 'leveraging generative artificial intelligence (AI) responsibly and ethically' and says Level 1 data can be processed, while barring confidential data; AI is allowed under data-classification conditions, so permit.

units.why: Purpose statement frames the standard as a foundation for 'leveraging generative artificial intelligence (AI) responsibly and ethically', an institution-wide framework (P56).
units.anchor: leveraging generative artificial intelligence (AI) responsibly and ethically
units.frag_start: To give guidance as a foundation for
units.policy: The standard gives guidance as a foundation for leveraging generative AI responsibly and ethically across all UTHSC environments.

units.why: Scope sentence fixes who is bound: 'members of the UTHSC community who have a need to access UTHSC IT Resources'; it sets scope, so P61.
units.anchor: applies to members of the UTHSC community
units.frag_start: This standard applies to members
units.policy: The standard applies to members of the UTHSC community who have a need to access UTHSC IT Resources.

units.why: Defines generative AI as 'a branch of artificial intelligence that enables machines to create original content', setting what the policy covers (P61).
units.anchor: enables machines to create original content
units.frag_start: Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) – a branch

units.why: Defines intellectual property in terms of putting proprietary or confidential information into generative AI without 'express written consent from all stakeholders'; it concerns what may be entered, so P50 over P52.
units.anchor: without express written consent from all stakeholders
units.frag_start: Intellectual Property - proprietary or confidential information
units.policy: Putting proprietary or confidential information, including unpublished research findings, internal university data or documents, or information protected by intellectual property rights, into generative AI requires express written consent from all stakeholders.
units.fit_note: Definition entry that implies a consent requirement.

units.why: Researchers must consider the nature and sensitivity of data 'before using generative AI to support research', a research-use rule (P62).
units.anchor: Researchers must consider the nature and sensitivity of scholarly data
units.frag_start: Researchers must consider the nature
units.frag_end: before using generative AI to support research.

units.why: Responsibilities section: researchers 'cannot put data that are confidential' into any generative AI without anonymization, risk evaluation and written consent; this is a data-protection rule (P50) aimed at research.
units.anchor: Researchers cannot put data that are confidential, contain sensitive information
units.frag_start: Researchers cannot put data that are
units.frag_end: express written consent from any other necessary parties.
units.policy: Researchers cannot put confidential or sensitive data, or data subject to legal or ethical requirements such as human subjects' data, into any generative AI without proper anonymization, evaluation of potential risks, and express written consent from any other necessary parties.

units.why: Names the Chief Information Security Officer as responsible for strategy, assessment and compliance of security standards; this assigns ownership of the policy domain (P80).
units.anchor: The Chief Information Security Officer (CISO) is responsible for providing strategy
units.frag_start: The Chief Information Security Officer (CISO)

units.why: Data owners must review and classify data in their area, 'Review and categorization'; role assignment for data governance (P80).
units.anchor: Data Owners are ultimately responsible for the data and information
units.frag_start: Data Owners are ultimately responsible
units.frag_end: Assign data classification based on the data’s potential impact level.
units.policy: Data Owners are responsible for the data and information collected and maintained by their department or division, reviewing and categorizing it and assigning data classification labels.
units.fit_note: Assigns data-owner duties for classification rather than naming who enforces the AI policy.

units.why: Users 'are responsible for complying with this Standard', a general compliance duty (P77).
units.anchor: Users of UTHSC IT Resources are responsible for complying with this Standard.
units.frag_start: Users of UTHSC IT Resources are

units.why: Practice item 1 requires adherence to the UT System acceptable use policy and UTHSC standard, which is following existing university policy (P77).
units.anchor: must adhere to the University of Tennessee System Administration (UTSA) acceptable use policy
units.frag_start: UTHSC Community members must adhere

units.why: Users should assume consumer products make data public, 'unless otherwise indicated', a privacy warning and tool-vetting cue (P50).
units.anchor: assume that all consumer generative AI products make data publicly available
units.frag_start: Users should assume that all consumer
units.frag_end: agreement with the University of Tennessee.

units.why: Unclassified data defaults to Level 3 'high-risk data by default'; a classification rule for what may be entered into AI (P50).
units.anchor: has not been explicitly classified is considered Level 3 or high-risk data by default
units.frag_start: All UTHSC data need to be classified
units.policy: All UTHSC data must be classified; data that has not been explicitly classified is considered Level 3 or high-risk data by default.

units.why: Level 1 data 'can safely process' in generative AI if it follows standards and ethical and reputational considerations; a permissive condition on public data (P50).
units.anchor: Generative AI can safely process publicly available information, general academic concepts
units.frag_start: Level 1 confidentially-ranked data – Generative AI
units.policy: Generative AI can safely process Level 1 data (publicly available information, general academic concepts, non-sensitive data), which must still comply with UTHSC standards and be considered relative to its ethical and reputational implications.
units.fit_note: Permits Level 1 data use; type P50 is about protection.

units.why: Level 2 or 3 data: 'Do not enter private or confidential data' including PII, FERPA, HIPAA data, research data and IP, so a data-protection ban (P50).
units.anchor: Do not enter private or confidential data
units.frag_start: Level 2 or Level 3 confidentially-ranked data –
units.policy: Do not enter private or confidential data, including personally identifiable information, information covered by FERPA, HIPAA or other regulations, research data and intellectual property classified as Level 2 or 3, into any generative AI product.

units.why: Users should 'Thoroughly anticipate the impact' because entered data cannot be removed; also warns about vague vendor 'AI' claims. Primary point is data caution (P50).
units.anchor: neither the individual who entered it nor the institution can directly remove it
units.frag_start: Thoroughly anticipate the impact of using
units.policy: Users thoroughly anticipate the impact of using generative AI before entering information into a tool, because once data is entered neither the individual nor the institution can directly remove it, and are cautious of vendor claims about AI.
units.fit_note: Also warns about vendor AI claims and unsupported performance.

units.why: Item 6 'Think critically. Evaluate and corroborate information' from AI tools is a verify-output rule (P31).

units.anchor: Some journals, offices, publishers, or educators may require that generative AI be cited
units.frag_start: Understand expectations. When using generative AI
units.policy: When using generative AI for writing support, users review the disclosure requirements of the publisher, reviewer or recipient of the finished product; some may require that generative AI be cited, potentially in different ways.
units.fit_note: Defers to the recipient's disclosure rules rather than requiring disclosure itself.

units.why: Item 8 'Stay informed. Follow conversations around AI technology' asks users to keep up with university guidance (P102).
units.anchor: Follow conversations around AI technology and further updates
units.frag_start: Stay informed. Follow conversations around AI

units.frag_start: Bias and unintentional harm: Generative AI

units.why: Risk item warns AI 'may produce or respond to content that is offensive, inappropriate, or violates ethical standards', a harm description (P53).

documents.title: Artificial Intelligence (AI) Tools
documents.summary: College policy that classes irresponsible or impermissible AI use as an Honor Code violation while leaving the decision to course instructors and, for theses, to advisors and committees. Instructors must state AI rules in the syllabus.
documents.stance_why: 'The ultimate decision for the use of AI tools in a course lies with the instructor(s)' and the research advisor and committee decide for theses; the college sets no default itself, so delegates.

units.why: Irresponsible or impermissible use 'will be considered a violation of the Honor Code and adjudicated by the Honor Council', classing misuse as misconduct (P36).
units.anchor: will be considered a violation of the Honor Code and adjudicated by the Honor Council
units.frag_start: Irresponsible or impermissible use of generative
units.policy: Irresponsible or impermissible use of generative AI tools in fulfilling curricular requirements will be considered a violation of the Honor Code and adjudicated by the Honor Council.

units.why: Irresponsible use includes 'failure to critically evaluate the accuracy of the generated content', making verification a student duty (P31).
units.anchor: failure to critically evaluate the accuracy of the generated content
units.frag_start: Irresponsible use of generative AI tools includes
units.policy: Irresponsible use of generative AI tools includes failure to critically evaluate the accuracy of the generated content (text, video or audio).

units.why: Impermissible use includes 'inappropriate citation' and use 'in violation of course instructions'; it defines misuse by reference to citation and course rules. Nearest type P36; the citation element is P24 but the unit defines misconduct.

units.frag_start: Impermissible use of generative AI tools includes
units.policy: Impermissible use of generative AI tools includes inappropriate citation of generated content and use of generated content in violation of course instructions.
units.fit_note: Also implies proper citation is expected and that course instructions bind.

units.why: States irresponsible use may spread misinformation and impermissible use 'may constitute plagiarism or cheating', linking misuse to misconduct (P36).
units.anchor: the impermissible use may constitute plagiarism or cheating
units.frag_start: Irresponsible use of generative AI tools may
units.policy: Irresponsible use of generative AI tools may result in the spread of misinformation, whereas impermissible use may constitute plagiarism or cheating.
